Comment: I completely agree. The Jones Act is the sole reason for the very high cost of living here.

For those not familiar, the Jones Act is a protectionist law that says any ship traveling from a U.S. port to a U.S. port must be an American-made ship with a majority American crew. So, a ship bringing goods to the U.S. from China is not allowed to stop in Hawaii, drop off part of its load, then continue on to another U.S. port. Since Hawaii's demand for goods is small (relatively speaking) what this does is forces ships to go past Hawaii to drop their goods on the Mainland. And goods that need to then go to Hawaii are offloaded from that foreign-flagged ship, loaded onto another U.S. flagged ship and then sent to Hawaii. Since over 80% of U.S. goods carried over water are on foreign-flagged vessels, and U.S. ships are generally much more expensive to operate, this more than doubles shipping costs to the islands.

Comment: Sure, Peggy, the 2006 NRC Committee recommended that the current MCL for fluoride should be lowered.  The sole reasons cited for this were risk of severe dental fluorosis, bone fracture, and skeletal fluorosis, with chronic ingestion of fluoride at a level of 4.0 ppm or greater.  It made no recommendation to lower the secondary MCL of 2.0 ppm.

a.  Severe dental fluorosis is rare in the US and, as noted by this same committee, does not occur in communities with a water fluoride content of 2.0 ppm, or less.  

b.  Risk of bone fracture is a U shaped curve with the greatest chance at too little or too much fluoride.  The least risk is at the optimal level.  

c.  Skeletal fluorosis is so rare in the US as to be nearly non-existent.  

As nearly 75% of the US is fluoridated at 0.7 ppm, lowering the MCL to a level between 2.0 and 4.0 ppm is a moot point.

FSA does not exist at the tap in fluoridated water. It is not ingested.  There is no need to test it for safety.

Steven D. Slott, DDS

Comment: In practice,  changes to a bill as recommended by the senate can be accepted, modified or rejected by the house and it has done all 3 over the years.

Also in practice, if the senate votes against a government bill then the house can try to reach a compromise in the bill that satisfies both parties and send the amended bill back to the senate for approval.  

But the house also is empowered to ignore the senate's opposition and to resubmit the bill to the upper chamber for final approval and passage.

For many decades, the senate has then speedily approved the bill the second time around.

This is known as The Doctrine of The Second Bite.

It ensures that the elected chamber has the final say as it should.

Most of this is not in the written constitution but rather is well established precedent.

So yes, the senate can delay the passage of bills and try to amend them but the ultimate authority is clearly in the house.

That means that most students are only in mandated testing six hours a YEAR. 

Any other acronym exam they take, STAR (for math) or SRI (for reading), are 15 minute, non-mandated, placement tests that help teachers drive instruction and aren't something kids can "opt-out" of just like a kid can't opt out of his US History midterm.

Comment: "It's all in how the research is designed."

That is absolutely true. I've also designed and conducted research in business when working while I was younger.

While an unethical researcher can design research to arrive at a predetermined outcome, I believe that is relatively rare. I think that most of the problems in research can be attributed to an array of factors such as poor sampling (size, quality, convenience, etc.), question design (what exactly is being measured?), response rates, schedule, cost, experience and so on.

Another issue concerns the consumer of the research. I've seen others in the situation where their results did not conform to the client's (or management's) beliefs. On one or two occasions I've even seen results twisted by the client to conform to those beliefs, even though the data clearly did not support.

I don't agree that all research is suspect. But all research has weaknesses, and it's best to be aware of that and look out for them.

(a.1) uses the title “engineer” or an abbreviation of that title in a manner that will lead to the belief that the person may engage in the practice of professional engineering; "is guilty of an offence" 

The provision doesn't seem to have been tested in court, but I suspect a good argument can be made that, while it might be risky for a person to hang out a shingle as an "engineer" without having a licence, he or she could act in-house under such a title. 

The main purpose of the provision is to protect the client and in the case of an in-house 'engineer' the client is fully aware.

Harm done? Zero.

Comment: If you are suing someone in the State of Oregon for negligence, you might be surprised what a court might say.  

Oregon is what they call a Comparative Fault/Negligence State, which means you can sue for negligence and the jury gets to  determine if both you and the other person were partly at fault.  

For example, you are crossing the street and get hit by a car but you were texting on your phone at the time.  A jury can say that you were 20% at fault and the motorist was 80% at fault.  So if they award $100,000, you would only get $80,000.   If they say you were 50% at fault and the other person was 50% at fault, nobody gets any money.

Hunger allows no choice
To the citizen or the police;
We must love one another or die.

Yet, dotted everywhere,
Ironic points of light
Flash out wherever the Just
Exchange their messages:
May I, composed like them
Of Eros and of dust,
Beleaguered by the same
Negation and despair,
Show an affirming flame.

Comment: Some more concepts:

A hurricane starts where there is a column of heated, moist air.  As the heated air rises, air has to be sucked in at the bottom to take its place.  The heated column of air functions just like a chimney.

It can only form where there is very little lateral (i.e., horizontal) shear in the wind column.  That is, hurricanes originate where the air in the center of the column is originally very nearly still, e.g., in the calm air in the doldrums.  If there is a strong wind constantly blowing the top off the heated air, a hurricane won't form.
.
Once the chimney is established, why does the air swirl in a helix?

This is not the right place for an explanation of conservation of angular momentum and coriolis force.  The gist of it is that it swirls for the same reason that water in a toilet bowl swirls.  The wind speed is highest near the core for the same reason that a figure skater spins faster when they hold their arms closest to their body.

Comment: Once you understand how the Canadian stumpage system works, it's hard not to see it as a government subsidy to the industry and workers.  Rather than auction off timber rights, under stumpage the BC government collects fees based on the lumber companies' difference between production cost and selling price.
Under an auction-based system (used in the USA), the lumber companies bear the risk of price fluctuations.  If prices drop due to excess supply, they are incented to reduce production.  However under stumpage, the Canadian producers have no incentive to reduce production, and their profit levels are assured, because if the lumber prices drop, the stumpage cost drops so they remain whole.  It is an insurance scheme for industry profits - they have transferred the risk to tax payers.  The gov collects less revenue from selling its wood, but what do they care so long as lumber companies and unions are happy?  No USA producers are upset, their gov won't backstop price drops.

However, nominal turnout is almost irrelevant.
.
B.C. has 4.770 m people
81% (3.864 m) are eligible to vote.
81.7% (3.157 m) registered.
56.9 % (1.797 m) voted.
.
True or absolute turnout was 1.797m/3.864m = 46.5 %, an all-time low.
(81.7% registration was also an all-time low.  Prior to voter ID, 90 - 92% was typical.)
.
In 2013 it was 47.4%.
In 2005 (before voter ID) it was 58%.
.
Vote suppression has many levels.
.
People are discouraged from registering;
Those registered are discouraged from voting;
Low information voters are encouraged to waste their votes, or to behave irresponsibly or short-sightedly.
.
These phenomena have been heavily studied.
.
At the end of the day, in the era of abuse of big data and narrow-cast online browser tracking and targeting, nominal turnout is a weak trend-revealing indicator, because it is a secondary or derivative indicator.
.
Absolute turnout, by contrast, is virtually always determinative.
